newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU formally agrees on pact on U.S.-Cuba trade dispute.
newsitem.headline: EU formally agrees on pact on U.S.-Cuba trade dispute.

text.p: European Union member countries formally agreed Friday to a deal with the United States to end a trans-Atlantic dispute over U.S. anti-Cuba laws.

A statement said that all 15 countries had told the EU headquarters in Brussels that they supported a plan that would end a formal disputes panel established at the World Trade Organisation over the Helms-Burton Act.
The act, an amalgam of U.S. anti-Cuba laws, has outraged Washington's trading partners because it threatens non-U.S. businesses that have interests in Cuba.

The European Commission and Washington agreed last week to negotiate a compromise policy towards Cuba under which the EU would drop its WTO complaint and work with the United States toward a global agreement on protection of expropriated property.
The United States, in exchange, would seek to change a key provision of Helms-Burton barring executives of companies that invest in disputed properties in Cuba from entering the United States.

On Wednesday EU ambassadors provisionally backed the plan but added a sharply worded statement warning Washington not to renege on the deal. EU governments had until Friday to endorse the ambassadors' decision.

France, Spain, Italy, Portugal and Belgium secured at Wednesday's meeting a clause that any backing of the deal be accompanied by the threat to reopen the WTO disputes panel if Washington took any action against EU companies.
The EU also restated its conclusions reached last July that the U.S. legislation towards Cuba, and other acts targeting Iran and Libya, were unacceptable both in law and in principle.

"Nothing in the understanding with the U.S. administration should be regarded as in any way detracting from the continuing approach to these issues set out in those conclusions," Friday's statement said.
